messages.subject: anagenetic events table question
messages.body_plain:
Hi BioGeo Group,

I have been looking through anagenetic events tables for individual runs of a BSM. My tree is stratified and the code for my BSM reflects this, yet the stratum column is populated only with 1s indicating that all anagenetic events are occurring in the 1st stratum of my tree(?). Does this reflect some built-in model constraint, could I be only retrieving part of these tables, or maybe I'm missing something more foundational about anagenetic dispersal within the models? I became more confused after seeing event timings that precede the first time-stratified bin in the abs_event_time column. Any thoughts?

Thanks for the help!
Chauncey Gadek

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] anagenetic events table question
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- that seems odd, although I could imagine that some datasets would have anagenetic events only in the top stratum.  Double-check that you are looking at the whole table, not just the top of it that is printed to screen, that the dates of the events are within the top stratum, and that you aren't confusing the overall tree strata with the "sub"-tree columns -- due to the complex nature of dealing with tree sub-pieces in APE/R/BioGeoBEARS, there is a lot of extra stuff.

Actually, given the absolute event dates you shouldn't need the stratum number at all, if that is looking screwy.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Looking at the table, it looks like you do have a few events that are older than 3 million years old, even though the apparent time bin they are in, according to table, is the 0-3 my time table.  I suspect that this is just the event copying information from the tip-node, and a tip branch that is longer than 3 million years could have a tip in the top time-bin, but an event older than that (if memory serves...I programmed this long ago, and the time-stratified stochastic mapping was rather more complex than regular stochastic mapping).

So, basically, I would recommend following the absolute event times and ignoring the time-bin labels, which are about the source tree structure I think.

Whether or not your results are plausible depends on the model/data/parameters being used, it's perfectly possible that for some combinations most of the dispersal/range expansion events happen high up in the tree, especially if its e.g. a DEC+J model with a reasonably high "d" estimated to explain some widespread tips.  I would have to run it myself to get a sense of it.  If you the example time-stratified BSM dataset/script from online, and see that it works OK (I'm pretty sure that produces some d events in older time bins), then probably it's working on your data also .

Cheers,
Nick

Hi -- oof, it looks like the fix to the Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping for super-low-probability histories isn't working for manually-set-up lists of ranges.

Fixing this would be a decent project, but a simpler solution for you, if you are getting 30/100 attempts succeeding already, is just increase the number of attempts by 3.5 times.  And/or, 50 BSMs is honestly 99% as good as 100 BSMs for most purposes.

Cheers!
Nick

I would disagree that it is "good" if all the methods support the same scenario!  Ideally, all the evidence/likelihood supports one model, and contradicts the rest of them!  Then, under a particular model, ideally one specific event history is supported, but often we aren't that lucky.  Note that even when DEC+J is very strongly supported, there are still a variety of specific historical scenarios that are possible, see Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping to visualize/measure the variability.  The pie charts are just a summary of this:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#stochastic_mapping

In your case, if AIC_wt is 0.87, this is what I would call "suggestive" evidence -- it is a little bit of evidence, not overwhelming evidence. See:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#interpreting_deltaAICs

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#ace_not_arr

The information for estimating the range at a node comes not just from the nodes above, but also from the ancestor node (which conveys information from the rest of the tree).
